# Chapter 7: Creating the Right Environment for Data-Aware Design

## Depth: Communicating Across Levels

One of the goals of designing with data is to avoid or diminish the necessity of "gut" decision making. Consequently, it can break hierarchical decision-making structures. The stereotype of management-led, top-down decision making based on hunches cannot flourish in a data-literate environment. Rather, company-wide data literacy that includes addressing well-formulated, carefully investigated questions, invites discussion, challenge, and most importantly the potential to be wrong.

Data is best when collected using any number of techniques (not just A/B testing, but also ethnographic field research, field deployments of prototypes, surveys, lab studies, usability research, etc.). Such grounded and carefully gathered user data can drive decisions, and is a less risky prospect than relying on hunches from individual executives working from a "gut feeling."

An early paper that focused on A/B testing published in 2007 by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield entitled "Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO" addressed this issue: data is an effective way to resolve conflicts in decision making without relying on rank, hierarchy, or company politics.

John Ciancutti, who worked at Netflix for a number of years, eventually as VP of Product Engineering, illustrates how data literacy across all roles at Netflix became a source of freedom and innovation within the company.

Patty McCord, who for over 12 years was the Chief Talent Officer at Netflix where she oversaw talent acquisition and HR, shows how an environment that embraces data can help its employees. Having a mechanism to measure whether you are doing the right thing for your customers allows for more people to have a voice in the development of the product.

One of the things that made the data-driven approach so successful at Netflix was that the practice of leveraging data was well established and universally accepted throughout the company. It may have started at the top with Reed Hastings and Neil Hunt (Netflix CEO and CPO) driving and believing in the value of leveraging data, but it was also embraced by everyone through management to the individual contributors on the team.

While at some companies the CEO might get to do whatever he wants, at Netflix Patty says it's different: everyone—including executives—can get caught up in thinking they know the answer. One of the reasons that embracing A/B testing can help to mitigate a top-down approach to problem solving is that everyone can learn from experimentation.

For example, when Reed would engage in product testing and had a strong idea for what he wanted to see in the product, he would submit his ideas to the same rigor of A/B testing as everyone else in the product team. On rare occasions, Reed might dictate the exact way that a product idea would work, but he would do this on "his test cell"; that is, on the experimental group in the test that he was backing. This cell would be tested against other cells that were proposed by the product team. If it didn't win, then it didn't get launched.

Having the upper-level management hold themselves accountable to the same process as the individual teams reinforced the practice of subjecting ideas, prototypes, features, and flows to grounded review through experimentation, and to the possibility of "failing" as a positive outcome. This value was central to a view of how the company should work.

If you are trying to shift into a data-aware framework, it will be critical to look at the way product and design decisions have been made to date. If these decisions were largely in the hands of one or two individuals, then it's worth taking the time to make sure that those people can understand and recognize the value of bringing in user/customer data into the decision-making process because they may find that their weight is diminished (as is the "weight" of any individual opinion). This is a good point to check with yourself as well—are you also comfortable and willing to see how incorporating data will change the weight of your own opinion within the design and product development process?

## Statistical Methods Overview

The chapter details the statistical techniques employed to test the research model relating DevOps capabilities to organizational outcomes. The primary analytical approach uses **Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM)**, which allows simultaneous estimation of measurement models (how constructs are operationalized) and structural models (relationships between constructs). This method is appropriate for exploratory research with complex models and was implemented using **PLS Graph** software (Chin 2001).

## Measurement Model Assessment

Construct reliability is evaluated using **Cronbach's alpha** and **composite reliability**, with thresholds of 0.70 indicating acceptable internal consistency. **Convergent validity** is assessed via average variance extracted (AVE), requiring values of 0.50 or higher to confirm constructs capture sufficient variance from their indicators. **Discriminant validity** is tested using the Fornell-Larcker criterion (comparing square roots of AVEs to inter-construct correlations) and cross-loadings to ensure constructs are empirically distinct.

## Common Method Bias

The chapter addresses common method variance—a significant concern in cross-sectional survey research where respondents provide data for both independent and dependent variables. **Harman's single-factor test** examines whether a single factor accounts for the majority of variance in the data. Additionally, **Lindell and Whitney's (2001) marker variable technique** provides a more rigorous procedural approach to detecting and controlling for method bias.

## Structural Model Evaluation

The structural model is assessed through path coefficients (standardized regression weights), their significance levels from bootstrapping procedures, and **R-squared values** indicating explanatory power for dependent constructs. Effect sizes (f²) measure the relative impact of predictor constructs.

## Sample and Survey Administration

The research utilized a cross-sectional survey administered to IT professionals, with standard mail and web-based protocols following Dillman's (1978) total design method to maximize response quality.

## Retirement Announcement and Public Response

BA framed retirement as a celebration, not a wake. They sought October coordination with Air France, but France declined—retiring in May, unwilling to sanction any dual celebratory exit post-accident.

BA used Forum 150 to brief top managers. The original 9th April 2003 date marked Concorde's 34th anniversary—switched to the 10th for optics. Bannister, in uniform, delivered the news via slide presentation. Roughly two-thirds expressed sadness, one-third relief—the "Marmite factor" presaging public response.

At the press conference, Bannister offered what became the universal party line: "It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons"—despite privately believing it had been the wrong decision at the wrong time for the wrong reasons.

BA had analyzed three Branson scenarios: success (BA blamed), failure (BA blamed for poor maintenance), or refusal (BA "beastly"). A senior Virgin pilot later told Bannister: "Thank God... because it would probably send us bust!"

**One Aircraft for Air Shows?**

Unlike the Vulcan operating on a "Permit to Fly," Concorde required a full Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate. Infrastructure costs of £60 million per annum would rise by £40 million—roughly a million weekly even halved. Airbus, focused on the A380's approaching first flight, refused to retain the Type Certificate. The air-intake computer technology remained proprietary and secret due to military aircraft applications.

**Shifting Public Discourse**

By summer, discussion moved from "why retire" to celebration of Concorde's legacy. Edward de Bono observed she appealed to both brain hemispheres—technologically superb yet artistically graceful. For Bannister, the simpler truth was that most Brits felt individual ownership: "That's my Concorde up there."

## Retirement Announcement and Public Response

The retirement was framed as a celebration, not a wake. BA initially sought to coordinate with Air France, proposing simultaneous retirement at end of summer (October). Air France declined, retiring in May instead—reflecting different attitudes and the reality that France would never sanction a celebratory dual retirement post-accident.

**The Announcement**

BA's internal briefing network "Forum 150" was chosen to announce retirement to top 150 managers. The original date, 9th April 2003, was the 34th anniversary of Concorde's first flight—switched to the 10th to avoid poor optics. Bannister, in uniform, delivered the news with a rehearsed slide presentation. The reaction split roughly two-thirds sad, one-third relieved—the "Marmite factor" that presaged public response.

At the subsequent press conference, when asked why Concorde was being retired, Bannister spontaneously offered the line that became universal party line: "It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons"—despite privately believing it had been the wrong decision at the wrong time for the wrong reasons.

**The Branson Question**

Anticipating Virgin Atlantic's interest, BA analyzed three scenarios: Branson succeeding (BA blamed), Branson failing (BA blamed for poor maintenance), or refusal (BA "beastly"). The official response—that government funding meant transfer wasn't BA's decision—contained enough truth to satisfy press. A senior Virgin pilot later told Bannister: "Thank God... because it would probably send us bust!"

**One Aircraft for Air Shows?**

Unlike the Vulcan operating on a "Permit to Fly" (lower certification), Concorde required a full Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate. Infrastructure costs of £60 million per annum would rise by another £40 million—roughly a million weekly even halved. Airbus, focused on the A380's approaching first flight, refused to retain the Type Certificate. The air-intake computer technology controlling engine airflow remained proprietary and secret due to military aircraft applications. No other organization realistically could have taken on the role.

**Shifting Public Discourse**

By summer, discussion moved from "why retire" to celebration of Concorde's legacy. Edward de Bono observed she appealed to both brain hemispheres—technologically superb yet artistically graceful. For Bannister, the simpler truth was that most Brits felt individual ownership: "That's my Concorde up there."

## Applying Habit Strategies to Business

The four laws of behavior change translate directly to organizational contexts. Leaders can engineer environments where productive habits become default through restructuring surroundings and embedding accountability.

Business-specific mechanisms include automating routine tasks, using habit contracts for accountability, and leveraging technology to reinforce desired behaviors. Tracking systems like decision journals help teams monitor habit formation. The framework restates the laws in workplace terms: making good habits obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying; making bad habits invisible, unattractive, difficult, and unsatisfying.

Measurement and reflection distinguish successful business habit strategies. Decision journals and habit contracts provide accountability data while reflection enables teams to refine approaches over time. Process-focused habits generate compounding improvements; outcome-only goals create short-term reactive cycles.

Organizations must balance habit standardization with necessary flexibility. Not all professional behaviors are suitable for rigid habit loops—strategic thinking may require deliberate variability. Excessive automation can reduce adaptability when conditions change.

Key examples include the Thorndikes' Massachusetts General Hospital cafeteria study (81–82), which demonstrated how environment design altered purchasing behaviors; Patterson and Ritty's cash register invention (171–72), which automated accounting and reduced theft; the Safeguard soap handwashing intervention in Pakistan (184–85), which proved principles work across cultures; Trent Dyrsmid's paper clip strategy (195–96); and Benjamin Franklin's journaling approach (196).
